hero.heading: I went looking for a faith I could actually live.
hero.lead: Homeward grew out of a long search: questions I could not ignore, years of study, retreats and monasteries across traditions, and an unexpected return to the Jesus I never really stopped loving.
hero.question: If God is love, is everyone who doesn’t believe exactly what I believe really going to hell?
hero.support: I could not find answers that satisfied both my mind and my heart. So I kept asking. Then I went looking.

questions.heading: I loved Jesus. I wasn’t sure what to do with the answers I was given.
paragraphs: I grew up evangelical. There was much in that world I still value: Scripture, prayer, service, the person of Jesus, and the conviction that faith should matter.

But some questions would not leave me alone. What happens to people in other religions? Is fear really the center of salvation? Why did a God of love sometimes sound so unlike the Jesus I encountered in the Gospels?

Rather than stop asking, I studied. I earned a degree with dual majors in Religious Studies and Anthropology and began trying to understand how human beings across cultures have sought God, meaning, transformation, and the sacred.

timeline.label: Inherited faith
timeline.title: A real love for Jesus—and real questions.
timeline.body: I did not go searching because I stopped caring. I went searching because the questions mattered.

timeline.label: Study
timeline.title: Religion + anthropology.
timeline.body: Academic study gave me language for culture, belief, ritual, sacred texts, and the many ways people make meaning.

timeline.label: Practice
timeline.title: Monasteries, retreats, silence, meditation.
timeline.body: Eventually I wanted more than ideas. I wanted to know what spiritual practice actually did to a human life.

search.heading: Not for a new label. For depth.
paragraphs: I traveled, stayed at monasteries and retreat centers, and practiced with people from Christian, Buddhist, Hindu, and non-denominational contemplative communities. I have done month-long retreat periods, 10-day silent meditation retreats, and retreats at places including Spirit Rock, Vajrapani, and Montserrat in Texas.

I learned the discipline of silence, attention, contemplation, solitude, and repeated practice. I did not adopt every belief I encountered. But I found practices that helped me become more awake—and, unexpectedly, helped me hear Christ again.

photos.alt: A large meditation hall during Shaun's years of retreat practice
photos.caption: Long retreat environments taught me what repetition, silence, and community can do to deepen a practice.

photos.alt: Shaun with retreat companions near a stupa
photos.caption: The search was experiential: learning with people, sitting in practice, and asking what actually transforms a life.

photos.alt: Friends and teachers gathered during spiritual formation
photos.caption: I was learning across traditions without pretending that every tradition says the same thing.
Christian contemplative voices helped me see that silence and meditation were not foreign to Christianity—they were part of its own deep tradition.

return.heading: My heart kept coming back to Christ.
paragraphs: Through all of it, I kept praying to Jesus. The person and way of Christ remained the deepest gravitational center of my spiritual life—even when my old framework for Christianity no longer held together.

Then voices within the Christian contemplative tradition began opening a wider door. Richard Rohr’s The Universal Christ was especially important. It gave me a way to understand Christ, salvation, creation, and divine love that felt expansive without asking me to abandon Jesus.

The practices I encountered elsewhere did not replace Christ for me. They taught me ways of silence, attention, contemplation, and solitude that ultimately helped me return to Christ with a more open heart.
return.book_body: It reframed Christianity for me in a way that felt both more spacious and more deeply centered in Christ.
return.quote: If I had heard Christianity framed this way earlier, I’m not sure I would have felt I needed to leave it to find depth.

missing.heading: I came home with practices. I didn’t have people to practice with.
missing.paragraph1: A retreat can open something in you. Then you come home, the phone rings, work starts, the kids need something, traffic happens—and the practice can quietly disappear.
missing.paragraph2: What I wanted was remarkably simple: a few people who wanted to keep going. A place to sit in silence together, explore Scripture honestly, try a practice during the week, come back and talk about what actually happened, and grow into real friendship along the way.
missing.signature: That is why I’m starting Homeward.

trust.eyebrow: YOU SHOULD KNOW WHO’S BEHIND THIS
trust.heading: A real person. A public life. No hidden spiritual persona.
trust.lead: Homeward is new. I think transparency matters more than pretending otherwise. I’m not asking you to trust an anonymous organization or a mysterious teacher.

cards.title: A real-world life.
cards.body: I lead Diamond Mattress, a fourth-generation family business. My professional history is public and easy to verify.

cards.title: Study, not special authority.
cards.body: I studied Religious Studies and Anthropology and have continued leadership, retreat, and personal-development work. I’m a serious student—not someone claiming spiritual perfection.

cards.title: A husband, father, and fellow traveler.
cards.body: I live an ordinary life with family, work, responsibilities, questions, and distractions. Homeward is meant for real life because that is where I need these practices too.

cards.title: No hidden ladder.
cards.body: Circles are currently offered at no cost. There is no secret teaching, expensive next level, pressure to agree, or expectation that Homeward replaces your church or tradition.

trust.community_heading: Homeward should never depend on me seeming impressive.
community_paragraphs: The point is not to build a community around Shaun. The point is to create a trustworthy container where people can experience God, practice the way of Jesus, ask honest questions, and support one another.
Over time, healthy community should become less founder-centered, not more.
is: Jesus-centered and open to sincere seekers.
Built around honest conversation and lived experience.
A community you can participate in season by season.
is_not: A replacement for church, therapy, or professional care.
A debate club or a place where everyone must agree.
A secret spiritual system or personality cult.
A claim that every tradition teaches the same thing.
A finished institution pretending it already has everything figured out.
trust.disclaimer: The retreat centers, traditions, books, and teachers referenced here are part of Shaun’s personal spiritual history. Their inclusion does not imply endorsement of Homeward.

final.eyebrow: IF THIS STORY SOUNDS A LITTLE LIKE YOURS
final.heading: Maybe we should have a conversation.
final.lead: You do not need to have your beliefs settled. You only need enough curiosity to explore what a practiced spiritual life could become.
